::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Quick refresher: the dot product

Multiply two lists of numbers position by position, then add the results.
For a drone with readings (22.8, 41) and weights (1.0, −0.1):
22.8 × 1.0 + 41 × (−0.1) = 18.7. One weighted score from one list of readings.
:::

## The problem

Before every flight, a ground crew checks a fleet of drones. Each drone reports
four readings: battery voltage, motor temperature, wind at the launch site and
payload weight. From those four numbers the crew wants two scores per drone:

- **Power margin:** how much energy headroom the flight has. High battery helps; heat, wind and payload eat into it.
- **Handling risk:** how hard the drone will be to control. Wind and payload push it up.

Each score is a weighted sum of the four readings, which is a
[dot product](dot-product.qmd). Three drones and two scores means
six dot products. A real fleet of 200 drones scored on 16 measures needs 3,200,
and a neural network layer does the same thing thousands of times per second.
Matrix multiplication is the bookkeeping that does all of them at once.

| Drone | Battery (V) | Motor temp (°C) | Wind (m/s) | Payload (kg) |
|:------|------------:|----------------:|-----------:|-------------:|
| A     | 22.8        | 41              | 6          | 1.2          |
| B     | 21.1        | 55              | 9          | 2.0          |
| C     | 23.4        | 38              | 3          | 0.5          |

: The readings, one row per drone {.striped}

The weights say how much each reading counts toward each score (they are
illustrative, not from a real flight manual):

| Reading      | Power margin | Handling risk |
|:-------------|-------------:|--------------:|
| Battery      | 1.00         | 0.00          |
| Motor temp   | −0.10        | 0.02          |
| Wind         | −0.30        | 0.50          |
| Payload      | −2.00        | 0.80          |

: The weights, one column per score {.striped}

## The picture

Stack the readings into a matrix **X** with one row per drone, and the weights
into a matrix **W** with one column per score. Every score is one row of X
dotted with one column of W. The only rule is that the row and the column must
be the same length, because each reading needs a weight.

## Play with it

The weights sit above the answer and the readings sit to its left, so every
answer cell lands exactly where its row and its column cross. Step through the
six cells, or click any empty answer cell to jump to it.

```{=html}
<matmul-stepper
  a='[[22.8,41,6,1.2],[21.1,55,9,2.0],[23.4,38,3,0.5]]'
  b='[[1.0,0.0],[-0.10,0.02],[-0.30,0.50],[-2.0,0.80]]'
  a-label="Readings X" b-label="Weights W" c-label="Scores XW"
  row-names='["Drone A","Drone B","Drone C"]'
  inner-names='["Battery","Motor temp","Wind","Payload"]'
  col-names='["Power margin","Handling risk"]'
  decimals="2"></matmul-stepper>
```

Notice what stays highlighted as you step across a row: the same drone's
readings are reused for every score. Step down a column and the same weights are
reused for every drone. That reuse is why GPUs can do this so fast.

## The math, minimal

The cell in row *i* and column *j* of the answer is row *i* of X dotted with
column *j* of W:

$$
(XW)_{ij} \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{n} X_{ik}\, W_{kj}
$$

- **Shapes:** an (m × n) matrix times an (n × p) matrix gives an (m × p) matrix.
  Here m = 3 drones, n = 4 readings and p = 2 scores.
- **Cost:** every answer cell takes n multiplications, so the whole product takes
  m · n · p of them. For the fleet: 3 × 4 × 2 = 24.
- **Order matters:** XW and WX are different. Here WX is not even defined, because
  (4 × 2) · (3 × 4) has inner sizes 2 and 3.

## Worked example

Drone B's power margin is row B of X dotted with the power-margin column of W:

| Reading    | Value | × Weight | = Contribution |
|:-----------|------:|---------:|---------------:|
| Battery    | 21.1  | 1.00     | 21.1           |
| Motor temp | 55    | −0.10    | −5.5           |
| Wind       | 9     | −0.30    | −2.7           |
| Payload    | 2.0   | −2.00    | −4.0           |
| **Total**  |       |          | **8.9**        |

Drone B has the lowest power margin of the three (A scores 14.5, C scores 17.7),
and you can see why: the hottest motors and the heaviest payload. Its handling
risk, 7.2, is also the highest, almost all of it from the 9 m/s wind.

## Run the code

The `@` operator in NumPy is matrix multiplication. Edit anything and press
**Run** (or Ctrl+Enter). Try raising Drone B's wind to 12 m/s and see which
scores move.

```{=html}
<py-cell packages="numpy"><script type="text/x-python">
import numpy as np

# One row per drone: battery (V), motor temp (C), wind (m/s), payload (kg)
X = np.array([[22.8, 41, 6, 1.2],
              [21.1, 55, 9, 2.0],
              [23.4, 38, 3, 0.5]])

# One column per score: power margin, handling risk
W = np.array([[ 1.00, 0.00],
              [-0.10, 0.02],
              [-0.30, 0.50],
              [-2.00, 0.80]])

scores = X @ W
print("shapes:", X.shape, "@", W.shape, "->", scores.shape)
print(scores.round(2))
print("Drone B power margin, one dot product:", round(X[1] @ W[:, 0], 2))
</script></py-cell>
```

Now scale up. The cell below scores 500 drones on 64 readings for 32 measures,
first with plain Python loops (one multiplication at a time) and then with `@`.
Both give the same answer; only the speed differs.

```{=html}
<py-cell packages="numpy"><script type="text/x-python">
import time
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
fleet = rng.normal(size=(500, 64))    # 500 drones, 64 readings each
weights = rng.normal(size=(64, 32))   # 32 scores

start = time.perf_counter()
loops = [[sum(fleet[i, k] * weights[k, j] for k in range(64))
          for j in range(32)] for i in range(500)]
t_loop = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
fast = fleet @ weights
t_fast = time.perf_counter() - start

print(f"multiplications: {500 * 64 * 32:,}")
print(f"Python loops: {t_loop:.3f} s")
print(f"numpy @:      {t_fast:.5f} s  ({t_loop / t_fast:,.0f}x faster)")
print("same answer:", np.allclose(loops, fast))
</script></py-cell>
```

One last picture: the three matrices as heat maps. Colour shows size, so you
can see which readings and weights drive each score.

```{=html}
<py-cell packages="numpy,matplotlib"><script type="text/x-python">
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

X = np.array([[22.8, 41, 6, 1.2], [21.1, 55, 9, 2.0], [23.4, 38, 3, 0.5]])
W = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [-0.10, 0.02], [-0.30, 0.50], [-2.0, 0.80]])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 3),
                         gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [4, 2, 2]})
for ax, M, title in zip(axes, [X, W, X @ W],
                        ["X  (3 x 4)", "W  (4 x 2)", "X @ W  (3 x 2)"]):
    ax.imshow(M, cmap="Blues" if M is X else "PuOr")
    for (r, c), v in np.ndenumerate(M):
        ax.text(c, r, f"{v:g}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
</script></py-cell>
```

## Where you'll see it

- **Every neural network layer.** A batch of inputs, shape (batch × inputs),
  times a weight matrix, shape (inputs × outputs). The
  [forward pass](../neural-nets/forward-pass.qmd) lesson is this lesson
  applied layer after layer.
- **Attention in transformers.** Comparing every word in a sentence with every
  other word is one matrix multiply, Q times K-transposed
  ([Q, K and V as tensors](../transformers/qkv-tensors.qmd)).
- **Navigation and graphics.** Rotating 10,000 points from a drone camera's frame
  into the world frame is one (10,000 × 3) · (3 × 3) multiply.
- **Finance.** Daily returns for many portfolios: (days × assets) times
  (assets × portfolios) gives every portfolio's return on every day.

## Check yourself

**1.** A batch of 64 images, each flattened to 128 numbers, goes through a layer
with 10 outputs. What shapes are the weight matrix and the result?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Weights (128 × 10). Result (64 × 10): one row per image, one column per output.
:::

**2.** Can you multiply a (3 × 4) matrix by a (3 × 2) matrix?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
No. The inner sizes are 4 and 3. Each row has 4 numbers but each column has
only 3, so there is nothing to pair the fourth number with.
:::

**3.** Which cell of the result holds Drone C's handling risk, and which two
things are dotted together to get it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Row 3, column 2. Drone C's row of readings dotted with the handling-risk column
of weights: 23.4 × 0 + 38 × 0.02 + 3 × 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.8 = 2.66.
:::

**4.** Doubling the number of drones doubles the work. What happens to the
work if you double the number of readings per drone instead?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
It also doubles. The cost is m · n · p, so each of the three sizes scales it
linearly. Doubling all three costs 8 times as much.
:::
